newsitem.title: MEXICO: Stockwatchers see solid Q3 growth in Mexico.
newsitem.headline: Stockwatchers see solid Q3 growth in Mexico.

text.p: Mexican stocks have allayed concerns that recent mid-term elections could trip up a galloping market and are poised to add to their gains in the coming weeks, analysts say.
Analysts were cautiously optimistic that recent volatility on the Brazilian market would not prove a lasting setback for Mexico.
As of Friday's close, the bourse's main IPC .MXX index had climbed 262.59 points, or 5.89 percent, for the month to date. Last week it closed down 2.1 percent at 4,720.56 points.

Although the ruling party lost its historic majority in the lower house of Congress, the July 6 vote pleased investors because it was seen as the cleanest in Mexico's history and a coming-of-age for the Mexican political system.

Share prices are expected to gain further in the coming weeks on positive international fund flows and expectations that a broad-based economic recovery will finally boost corporate earnings in the third quarter, they added.
"The elections are behind us now, and fundamentals are good," said Todd Edwards, an investment strategist at the Latinvest brokerage.
Several analysts said imminent second quarter corporate earnings were expected to improve on the first quarter and herald strong earnings growth in the second half of the year.
"Second quarter earnings will be encouraging, but they won't knock the ball out of the park...We're expecting big earnings in Q3," Edwards said.
"Mexico is entering a good stage in the business cycle. Growth is moving from exports and investment and broadening to consumption," he added.
Lars Schonander, research head at Santander Investment in Mexico, had a more sanguine view of second quarter reports, but agreed things could be going Mexico's way.
"We are watching out for negative surprises (in second quarter reports) rather than anything exciting," he said.
"(But) the numbers may not matter given the favourable (interest) rate environment for Mexico," he added. "Mexico still looks reasonably cheap compared to the region and other emerging markets."

Gerardo Copca, of the Valores Finamex brokerage, said early second quarter reports tended to show Mexican shares had cheapened in terms of multiples since the first quarter, despite recent sharp gains in prices.
"They are trading at cheaper price-to-earnings and price-to-book value multiples, and that's what investors buy on," he said.

The analysts did not rule out a repeat of the "samba effect" -- recent volatility on the Mexican bourse in sympathy with falling share prices in Brazil -- but said the impact was likely to be temporary.
The Bovespa index of most active stocks in Sao Paulo dived 547 points to 11,617 -- triggering a fall of 95.81 points by the IPC to 4,720.56.
Copca said Mexico was not as susceptible as Brazil to the perception that its currency is overvalued.

"If there is a margin of overvaluation at all, it is minimal compared to Brazil. We've been through the debate as to whether the peso is overvalued," he said, referring to the fumbled December 1994 devaluation that sent Mexican financial markets into a tailspin.
"A devaluation in Brazil could hit us for a while, but it could then switch fund flows to Mexico," he added.
In Mexico, a devaluation of the Brazilian real is seen as a distant possibility, though in Brazil market analysts say chances of such a development are nil.
Edwards also said funds were increasingly likely to flow to Mexico due to higher global liquidity in the wake of declining interest rates.
"My guess is that money will increasingly go to Mexico and portfolio weightings will shift that way," he said. "From a capital flow scenario, Mexico looks fantastic."
